one_liner: Krovetz's AES-NI code for AEZ v4, a nonce-misuse-resistant AEAD, uses ~2.7x fewer cycles than AES-256-GCM, but v4 is broken.
what_it_does: AEZ (Hoang, Krovetz, Rogaway; CAESAR third round) authenticates and encrypts by appending abytes zero bytes to the plaintext and then enciphering the whole string with a wide, variable-length blockcipher tweaked by the nonce, AD and abytes. The result is robust AE: nonce reuse leaks only whether messages repeat, and any ciphertext expansion can be chosen. This entry is SUPERCOP's crypto_aead/aezv4/aesni (AEZ v4.1, Ted Krovetz, 2015), exposed only through the SUPERCOP crypto_aead_encrypt/decrypt API with a 48-byte key, 12-byte nonce and 16-byte tag. Internally there are aez_setup/aez_encrypt/aez_decrypt functions that take a context. It is not an AES-GCM replacement: the algorithm, key size and security model are all different.
how_it_is_fast: It follows the designers' 'prove-then-prune' approach. The provably secure AES-based tweakable blockcipher is swapped for AES4 (four aesenc rounds keyed directly by the 128-bit subkeys I, J and L, with no key expansion) in most calls, and full 10-round AES is kept only for a few blocks per message. AEZ-core is an EME/OTR-style encipher-mask-encipher over pairs of blocks: five AES4 calls per 32 bytes, i.e. about 10 AES rounds per 16-byte block and close to AES-CTR cost, against 14 rounds plus a GHASH multiply per block for AES-256-GCM. Per-block offsets come from XE-style doubling in GF(2^128), and pass one keeps 16 blocks (8 independent pairs) in flight per iteration to saturate the AES-NI pipeline. AD goes through an AES4-based universal hash (0.17 vs 0.32 cpb for GCM on 0+long). Forgeries are rejected after the first pass (0.15 vs 0.26 cpb on long+long).
when_to_use: Reproducing or analysing CAESAR-era eBACS/SUPERCOP AEAD results. It is a well-measured, readable (~900-line) AES-NI implementation of a wide-block AEAD.

As the starting point for studying or porting AEZ's AES4 + EME-style structure. For anything that encrypts real data, use the AEZ v5 code instead, which runs at essentially the same speed on the same page (0.28 vs 0.26 cpb long+long encrypt).

The use cases AEZ targets (with v5): nonce reuse or nonce-less designs where you need misuse resistance at roughly AES-CTR cost, messages that fit in memory, and small packets, where AEZ is about 4x cheaper than AES-256-GCM at 64+64 bytes (1.18 vs 4.70 cpb).
Decrypt paths that are flooded with forgeries: invalid ciphertexts are rejected at about half the cost of a valid decrypt (0.15 cpb long+long forgery).
when_not_to_use: Any real deployment. The v4 specification, which this code implements, has an offset-collision bug in its tweakable blockcipher: two different tweaks get the same offset. It was found by Bonnetain, Derbez, Duval, Jean, Leurent, Minaud and Suder (2017), who showed easy forgeries. The designers say this destroys authenticity (and probably privacy), and fixed it only in AEZ v5.
Protocols that need a standard, interoperable AEAD (TLS, IETF, FIPS). AEZ never became a standard and was not in the CAESAR final portfolio.

Streaming or online encryption, and messages of 4 GiB or more. As an MRAE scheme it needs two passes over the whole message, and this code converts lengths to 32-bit unsigned, so they silently truncate.

Builds without AES-NI + SSE4.1 or ARMv8 Crypto Extensions, including MSVC, where __AES__ is not defined. The file hits #error, and the portable ref implementation took about 70x longer than aesni in eBACS's test-time column.

High-volume keys or conservative security margins. Security holds only to the birthday bound, and key-recovery birthday attacks exist (Fuhr-Leurent-Suder 2015; Chaigneau-Gilbert 2016, which targets v4.1). The spec caps use at 2^48 bytes per key, and AEZ itself has no proof, because the AES4 substitution is heuristic.

integration.form: source-drop (a single crypto_aead/aezv4/aesni/encrypt.c plus api.h in SUPERCOP layout; outside SUPERCOP you must supply a crypto_aead.h shim)
integration.dependencies: none (a reference BLAKE2b is bundled and used only to derive subkeys from keys that are not 48 bytes)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 on GCC or Clang with -maes -msse4.1 (or -march=native) so that __AES__ is defined. eBACS builds it with Clang 19.1.7 and GCC 14.2.0 at -O/-O2/-O3/-Os; MSVC is unsupported.
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AES-NI + SSSE3/SSE4.1; AArch64 with ARMv8 Crypto Extensions (__ARM_FEATURE_CRYPTO); anything else needs the slow portable ref implementation
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The SUPERCOP entry points build a fresh aez_ctx_t on the stack for every call and are reentrant, but the internal aez_hash writes ctx->delta3_cache, so a shared context must not be used from several threads at once.

gotchas: Out-of-bounds reads. Encryption loads the 16 bytes after the end of the message and masks them off. The 12-byte nonce and the partial last AD block are fetched with full 16-byte loads. GCC 14 on eBACS warns about a read at offsets 33-48 of the 48-byte pad[] table. Pad your buffers, or expect ASan reports and possible faults at page boundaries.

The SUPERCOP wrapper hard-codes a 48-byte raw key (I||J||L, with no key schedule), a 12-byte nonce and a 16-byte tag. aez_hash handles only nonces and abytes up to 16 and a single AD string, although the spec allows vector AD and arbitrary lengths.
eBACS marks it 'T:' (constant time not declared as a goal; the build symbol is crypto_aead_aezv4_aesni_timingleaks_*), while the aes256gcmv1 baseline has no such mark.
Its ciphertexts do not match AEZ v5 or any other version: v5 changed the offset definition, so data encrypted with this code cannot be decrypted by v5 code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Of the siblings measured on the same eBACS page, AEZ is the only one that is nonce-misuse-resistant, so it (as v5, not this v4 code) is the choice only when nonce reuse must be survivable. For pure speed, AEGIS-128L is faster (0.21 vs 0.26 cpb long+long encrypt; 0.97 vs 1.18 cpb at 64+64), and so is Tiaoxin-346 on encrypt (0.15 cpb).
verified_claims_summary: The measurement is eBACS supercop-20260627 on 'freshwrap,big', an Intel Core 5 210H (Raptor Cove P-cores, 2.2 GHz). aezv4/aesni was built with clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O and aes256gcmv1 (fastest build: Dolbeau's AES-NI intrinsics) with clang -O2. Median long+long cost was 0.26 vs 0.70 cpb for encrypt (~2.7x) and 0.26 vs 0.57 for decrypt (~2.2x). Derived from the page data: message-only long+0 encrypt was 0.35 vs 1.07 cpb (~3.1x), 1536+1536 encrypt 0.31 vs 0.82 (~2.6x), and 64+64 encrypt 1.18 vs 4.70 (~4x).
status_note: The mirror is an abandoned 2016 snapshot of Krovetz's public-domain (Unlicense, and the spec says 'no AEZ-related patents have been or will be requested') code that current SUPERCOP still builds, so it is easy to copy, but it implements a spec the designers withdrew in March 2017, so treat it as a benchmark artifact and use AEZ v5 instead.
